passage:
Thursday. Something's off with Ganga, and I'm tired of pretending it isn't. For a month she's been 'at the library' till ten, but her library card shows no entries, she's changed her phone password, and last Sunday she flinched when a message popped up. Every time, I make an excuse for her. Exams. Stress. I'm being paranoid. Then I lie awake doubting myself. Today Meera asked me, 'If a friend told you all this, what would you say?' I'd say: that's not paranoia, that's noticing. I thought about reading her messages while she slept. I didn't. That's not who I want to be. So tonight at the tea stall I asked her straight: 'Ganga, things have changed. The late nights, the password, the flinch. Is there something you need to tell me?' She went quiet for a long time. Then she said, 'Can we talk tomorrow? Properly.' My stomach dropped. But at least I asked.
- Anand

qa.a: At the library.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling while lying awake?
qa.a: Anand felt anxious and full of self-doubt, making excuses for Ganga while sensing something was wrong.

qa.q: What did Anand do instead of spying?
qa.a: Trusted what had been observed and asked Ganga directly and calmly at the tea stall.

qa.a: As noticing real changes, not paranoia.

grounding: A diary of a young person doubting themself as a partner's behaviour changes, trusting their observation and asking directly instead of spying or excusing it.

So when Ankita saw Vaibhav's red scooter parked outside the college canteen three evenings in a row, with Vaibhav inside holding hands with a girl from the commerce batch, she knew what it meant. Vaibhav's fiancée, Sunita, taught at Ankita's old school and had once given her extra maths classes for free. Ankita felt sick. At the bus stop, two girls were already whispering about it. One asked her, 'You know him, na? Tell us!' Ankita shook her head. 'Not my story to spread.' That night she messaged Vaibhav: 'I saw you at the canteen. I'm not going to gossip. But Sunita deserves the truth, and it should come from you, soon.' He called her, angry at first, then quiet. 'I know,' he said at last. Ankita slept badly, torn between loyalty to him and fairness to Sunita. If he hadn't told Sunita in a week, she decided, she would think again.

passage:
Dear Madhuri,
I need to tell someone who won't judge me, so here it is.
There's a man at my internship, Karan, who is engaged. We've been staying late together on the same project, and lately he's been texting me at night. Long messages, about how his fiancée 'doesn't understand him' and how I do. And honestly, I've loved it. I've felt special, chosen. For a few weeks I told myself this was different, that the rules didn't apply to something this real.
Then on Saturday I saw his fiancée's photos online. She looked kind. She was holding a card that said '3 months to go!' And I felt sick.
I'd be hurting her, and I'd be setting myself up to be the next one he lies to.
So I've stopped replying to the night texts. I've asked my manager to move me to the other project team. It hurts more than I expected.
Can you come over Sunday? I don't want to be alone with my phone.
Pooja

qa.a: '3 months to go!'

qa.q: How had Pooja felt about Karan's night texts?
qa.a: Pooja felt special and chosen, loving the attention.

qa.q: What steps did Pooja take to step back?
qa.a: Stopped replying to the night texts, asked to move to another project team, and reached out to Madhuri for support.

qa.a: Deeply hurt and betrayed, since she's counting down to the wedding.

passage: Dhruv, you asked why I left the theatre group. It's because of Tanya. I'm Jeevan, and I fell for someone who's in a relationship. Four years with her boyfriend. At rehearsals we'd laugh at the same jokes and walk to the bus together, and she'd say things like, 'You get me in a way he doesn't.' I started telling myself stories. That our connection was different. That she'd leave him. That the usual rules didn't count because this felt so real. Then one night she kissed me outside the auditorium, and afterwards she cried and said she couldn't lose him. I went home and felt hollow. I realised I'd been lining up to get hurt, and to help hurt someone I'd never even met. So I told her we couldn't keep doing this. I stepped back from theatre for a term so I wouldn't keep circling. It was hard. I miss the stage. But I don't want to be the secret in someone else's story.

Wednesday night. I still can't believe I'm writing this. Baljeet is engaged. Engaged! His fiancée, Simran, messaged me today: 'Are you seeing my fiancé?' She'd found my photos on his phone. For eight months he told me he was single, that his family 'had no plans' for him. My hands shook so badly I dropped my chai. First I was furious at Simran, for some reason, as if she'd stolen something. I typed a nasty reply. Then I stopped. She didn't lie to me. He did. She's been lied to as well, probably for longer than me. So I wrote back: 'I didn't know. I'm so sorry. He told me he was single.' Then I blocked Baljeet everywhere. I called Didi and cried for an hour. I'm so angry I can barely breathe, and I have every right to be. But I'm not going to fight the wrong person.
- Pallavi

I need us to really talk, or to be honest that it isn't working.' There was a long silence. Then Nikhil said, 'I've felt it too. Let's talk properly this weekend.'

You notice it, and you choose what to do. So I've decided. I said no to the coffee, politely. I'll keep things strictly about work with him. And tonight I'm cooking Farida's favourite biryani, not out of guilt, just because I want to be here. Noticing someone isn't cheating. Feeding it would be.

passage: By Tuesday the whole hostel seemed to know that Ritu's boyfriend had cheated. In the mess, girls she barely knew stopped her: 'We should post his chats, everyone should see what he is.' Someone had already made a meme with his photo, and it was circulating in the batch group. Ritu felt humiliated, as if her pain had become a show. She pushed her plate away and went back to her room. Ishita, her roommate, knocked a few minutes later. 'Do you want me to shut this down?' Ritu nodded, tears finally falling. Ishita messaged the batch group: 'Please delete the meme. This is Ritu's private pain, not entertainment.' Then she sat on the floor with her. Ritu said, 'I'm so angry at him. But I don't want to humiliate him online. That's not who I am.' 'Then don't. Tell me instead. And your sister. That's enough people.' That night Ritu turned off her notifications and called her sister.

passage:
Dear Zubin,
I know you posted those screenshots of Anika's messages because you were angry on my behalf. I know you meant it as loyalty. Thank you for caring that much.
But please take the post down today.
I've been reading the comments, and they make me feel worse, not better. People I don't even know are calling her names, and some are asking me for 'the full story'. My hurt has turned into something everyone can watch. I didn't want that. What she did broke something in me, and I'm still angry. But humiliating her in public doesn't undo it, and I don't want to become someone who uses his pain as a weapon.
What would help is exactly what you did on Sunday night, before the post: sitting in my room with bad tea and letting me talk. I need a few people who'll listen, not a crowd.
Can you come over tomorrow?
Siddharth

passage: When Chaitanya ended things last March, on a Wednesday, in a café near college, I thought I would never feel normal again. I'm Farida, and I spent the next two weeks trying to find the reason. Was it my laugh? My exams? The fight about his cousin's wedding? I made lists. I reread two years of messages at 3 a.m., looking for the moment it went wrong. I drafted long texts begging for one more chance, and deleted them, thank God. I felt worthless, as if someone had officially declared me not enough. What helped wasn't finding the reason. There wasn't one perfect reason; he'd said he just didn't feel it any more. What helped was my friends Salma and Neetu sleeping over three nights in a row, letting me cry and eat terrible pizza and cry again. Somewhere in there, I stopped searching and just grieved. By June I laughed properly for the first time. I still don't know exactly why. I don't need to.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya say was the reason?
qa.a: He just didn't feel it any more.

qa.q: How did Farida feel in the weeks after the break-up?
qa.a: Farida felt worthless and confused, as if officially declared not enough.

qa.q: What helped Farida more than searching for a reason?
qa.a: Grieving openly and leaning on Salma and Neetu, who stayed over three nights in a row.

passage: The university sports complex was nearly empty at six, just the thud of a basketball from the far court. Keerthana had asked Baljeet to meet her on the bleachers, not over text. For weeks she'd been drafting ways to fade out: slower replies, 'busy with exams', letting it die quietly. But she knew how that would feel from his side. When he sat down, smiling, her stomach twisted. 'Baljeet, I need to be honest. I've thought about this a lot. I want to end our relationship.' His smile fell. 'Did I do something?' 'No. You didn't do anything wrong. I just don't feel the way I did, and I don't think that's coming back. I didn't want to lie or disappear.' He was quiet. 'Can we try?' 'I don't want to give you false hope. I'm sorry.' She stayed while he sat with it. Walking home, she felt guilt and, under it, a clear, quiet relief.

qa.q: Where did Keerthana meet Baljeet?
qa.a: On the bleachers of the university sports complex.

qa.q: What did Keerthana feel walking home?
qa.a: Guilt, and underneath it, a clear, quiet relief.

qa.a: She told Baljeet face to face, honestly, without blaming him or giving false hope, and stayed while he took it in.

passage:
Dear Didi,
I did it tonight. I ended things with Ayesha.
You told me not to text it, so I didn't. I asked her to meet at the chai place near her PG. My hands were shaking. I told her the truth: I care about her, but I haven't been happy for months, and I don't see us going forward. I didn't list her faults, even though part of me wanted to, just so I'd feel less like the bad guy. When she asked if we could take a break instead, I said no, gently, because a break would just be false hope.
She cried. I felt awful. I still do. I kept wanting to take it back just to stop her crying. But I also walked home feeling lighter than I have since January, which makes me feel even more guilty.
I think I did it as kindly as I could. Is it normal to feel relieved and terrible at the same time?
Ojas

qa.q: Where did Ojas meet Ayesha?
qa.a: At the chai place near her PG.

qa.q: What did Ojas feel walking home?
qa.a: Relieved and lighter, and at the same time guilty and terrible.

qa.a: Met face to face, explained his feelings without listing her faults, and refused a break to avoid false hope.

qa.q: How did Ayesha respond?
qa.a: She cried and asked if they could take a break instead.

grounding: A letter from a young man who ends a relationship face to face, honestly and without blame or false hope, feeling both relief and guilt.

passage: Three weeks after Harsha left, Indu still couldn't walk past the vada pav stall near Dadar station without her throat closing. It was where they'd had their first proper conversation, both soaked from the rain. The bookshop, the bus stop, even a song on the radio in an auto: everything was a trapdoor. She cried in the office washroom twice that week. At night she scrolled until 3 a.m., watching episode after episode so she wouldn't have to feel anything, and one friend kept suggesting she 'get back out there' with a dating app. On Saturday her roommate Swara sat on her bed. 'Indu, this is grief. Real grief. Treat it like that.' So they made a small plan: sleep by midnight, actual meals, a walk along the sea face every evening, and one friend to talk to each day. No apps for now. It didn't fix anything. But by the next week, the vada pav stall only stung instead of knocking her down.

qa.a: At the vada pav stall near Dadar station.

qa.q: How does Swara see what Indu is going through?
qa.a: As real grief that deserves to be treated as grief, not numbed away.

grounding: Shows a young woman grieving a break-up, moving from numbing and rebound pressure to sleep, food, movement and talking.

passage:
'You've gone on three dates this week,' Ankita said, setting two cups of tea on the hostel steps. 'Three. You and Dechen broke up nine days ago.'
Tenzin shrugged. 'Moving on.'
'Are you, though? You cried at the momo stall on Tuesday.'
'The chilli was strong.'
'Tenzin.'
He was quiet. Then: 'Everything reminds me of her. The library, the momo stall, the bus to Majnu ka Tilla. If I stop for one minute, it hits me. So I don't stop.'
'That's grief. You're allowed to have it.'
'It feels pathetic.'
'It's not. It's what happens when something mattered. But dating people so you don't feel it isn't fair to them, or to you.'
He stared at his tea. 'So what do I do?'
'Boring stuff. Sleep. Eat real food, not just instant noodles. Come for football on Sunday. And talk. To me, to your brother. Cry if you need to.'
'That's it?'
'That's it. It's slow. It works.'

qa.q: How long ago did Tenzin and Dechen break up?
qa.a: Nine days ago.

qa.q: Why does Tenzin avoid stopping for even a minute?
qa.a: Because the grief hits him whenever he stops, and feeling it seems pathetic to him.

qa.q: What does Ankita suggest instead of rebound dating?
qa.a: Sleep, eat real food, come for football on Sunday, and talk to her and his brother, crying if needed.

qa.q: How might the people Tenzin dated this week be affected?
qa.a: They may be hurt or misled, since he's dating to avoid feeling rather than out of real interest.

grounding: Shows a young man grieving a break-up who uses rebound dates to numb it, and a friend helping him treat it as real grief.
